deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair-copy of lecture or study notes on ancient Greek history, continuing the narrative of the Persian Wars from the previous page and running on into the next. The hand and content suggest school or university history notes, possibly in the style of Heeren's Göttingen lectures. Whether Gauss wrote them himself (perhaps from his youth) or a family member or student did cannot be decided from this page alone.

The content, in order:
- Xerxes advances to Thermopylae; Leonidas falls on '6 July 480'.
- An indecisive naval engagement off Cape Artemisium.
- Themistocles withdraws into the bay of Salamis.
- The battle of Salamis on '23 Sept. 480'. The Greek fleet numbers 380 ships against a much larger Persian fleet, and the Greeks win.
- Xerxes hurries back to Asia, leaving the core of his army under Mardonius in Thessaly (479).
- Mardonius advances. The Greeks, having had time to prepare, field 110,000 men. Aristides commands (the Athenians) and Pausanias holds the supreme command.
- Mardonius builds a fortified camp near Plataea. In the battle there the Greeks win, Mardonius is killed, and the camp is stormed the same day ('25 Sept. 479').
- The Greek fleet, sent to Asia Minor to stop Persian reinforcements, wins at Cape Mycale on the same day. The Persian fleet is burned, Greece gains supremacy at sea, and 'national spirit' is aroused.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Historical, not mathematical. The dates '6 July 480' (Thermopylae), '23 Sept. 480' (Salamis) and '25 Sept. 479' (Plataea/Mycale) follow an older 18th/19th-century chronology. Modern reckoning puts Thermopylae in about August/September 480, Salamis in late September 480, and Plataea/Mycale in about August 479.

'Mardonius rückte ohne Widerstand vor bis Plataeae' compresses events. Mardonius first reoccupied Athens, then withdrew to Boeotia and fortified a camp on the Asopus. The Greeks then advanced to face him.

The '380 ships' at Salamis and the '110000 Mann' at Plataea are Herodotus' figures (378 ships; 110,000 men). Modern historians regard them as approximate or inflated, but the notes report them faithfully.
'um zu verhindern daß keine persische Truppen' is an archaic double negative, not a factual error.

The next page's statement that the war continued 30 more years leads from 479 BC to about 449 BC (Peace of Callias)
